faqs.q: What are flying squirrels, and are they in my Tallahassee attic?
faqs.a: Southern flying squirrels are small, nocturnal, gliding squirrels — common in Tallahassee's oak hammocks and almost unknown to the homeowners they live above. Signs are light pattering and rolling acorns in the attic late at night, and droppings smaller than a gray squirrel's. They enter through gaps as small as a quarter, so their exclusion is a fine-mesh, whole-roofline job, done with one-way exits. They are native and social; the answer is exclusion, thoroughly sealed — and they are a good reminder that not every attic noise is a gray squirrel.

Winter drives squirrels, rats, and flying squirrels into attics with purpose; spring brings chimney raccoons; and the Panhandle species set applies — copperheads in the hammock leaf litter, timber rattlesnakes in the northern pine woods, and skunks as common residents. faqs.q: Can you relocate a raccoon from my Bradfordville attic?
faqs.a: Only on Florida's strict conditions. Under FWC Rule 68A-9.010, a live-captured native animal must be released or handled within 24 hours, and an off-site release is lawful only within the same county, on 40 or more contiguous acres, with the release landowner's written permission — or it can be released on-site once the home is sealed. Raccoons are Florida's most-reported rabies carrier, so we never promise a casual drop-off in the woods, and nonnative animals such as iguanas and Muscovy ducks may never be relocated at all.

faqs.q: Bats come out of a sinkhole near my Woodville home — should anything be done?
faqs.a: About the sinkhole, no — cave and sinkhole bat roosts are natural karst features, the bats are beneficial and protected by the same exclusion-season law that covers buildings, and disturbing a natural roost is neither lawful nor wise. About your house, yes: if bats shift from the sinkhole to your attic, that colony gets identified — southeastern myotis is a cave species of conservation concern in this region — and any exclusion is planned carefully in the legal window with the species in mind. Natural roosts get respect; house colonies get craftsmanship.

faqs.q: How do I keep raccoons out of my Chaires chicken coop?
faqs.a: Build the coop like a raccoon is inspecting it, because one will. Hardware cloth (never chicken wire) on all openings, a buried apron or solid floor against digging, two-step latches a raccoon's hands cannot work, and feed locked in metal cans. Then trap the raccoons currently working the property, checked daily, released on your land or in-county under the 40-acre permission rule. Coops hardened this way in Chaires typically go quiet within a week, and stay quiet.

faqs.q: Our Fort Braden camp sits empty for weeks — how do we protect it?
faqs.a: Seal it like a boat left in the water: completely, or expect boarders. Raccoons and squirrels test empty camps within days, and a colony can do a season's damage before the next visit. We audit the whole structure — roof, vents, crawl access, chimney — seal with gnaw-proof materials, and leave you a photo record. Add a pre-arrival check habit: walk the roofline visually before unpacking, and any new hole found early is a small fix instead of an attic colony.
